title: “From Unseen Needs to Classroom Solutions”: Exploring AI Literacy Challenges & Opportunities with Project-Based Learning Toolkit in K-12 Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines the challenges and opportunities of supporting AI literacy in K-12 classrooms through a Project-Based Learning (PBL) toolkit. The authors ask how teachers understand AI literacy, how they adapt AI tools into lesson plans, and how teachers’ and students’ backgrounds shape perceptions of AI tools and classroom use. The motivation is to make AI education more accessible beyond computer science, especially in interdisciplinary subjects where teachers may have limited technical expertise.

The intervention studied is a prototype PBL AI literacy toolkit containing three tools: an AI Art Lab, AI Music Studio, and AI Chatbot. Teachers used a short demo video, explored the toolkit, and then participated in semi-structured interviews and co-design sessions. The study involved 13 middle- and high-school teachers teaching a range of subjects in North America and East Asia, across public, private, and charter schools. Teachers designed hypothetical classroom activities using the toolkit for subjects such as math, science, Chinese, social studies, art, biology, and IT.

Findings suggest teachers generally viewed AI as useful for self-directed learning, creativity, inquiry, and concept reinforcement, but they also worried about accuracy, trustworthiness, copyright, and uneven student readiness. The toolkit was seen as especially helpful for scaffolding student exploration, supporting personalized learning, and reducing barriers for teachers with limited AI knowledge. The authors conclude that modular, adaptable, and scaffolded AI tools can support AI literacy across diverse K-12 settings, while further teacher training and better onboarding are needed for broader adoption.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model/chatbot system used for conversational question answering, prompt evaluation, and generating text, images, music, and other AI-assisted outputs. The paper discusses it as part of a broader PBL AI literacy toolkit rather than naming a specific commercial product.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in the toolkit as an AI Chatbot for student Q&A, concept reinforcement, prompt evaluation guidance, and conversational tutoring; also discussed alongside other toolkit tools in teacher co-design interviews.

findings.finding_summary: In qualitative interviews with 13 middle and high school teachers, the AI chatbot was the most widely adopted toolkit component (n=9 for course designs). Teachers said it could function as a 24/7 tutor, help students clarify misunderstandings outside class, provide supportive non-judgmental practice, and save teacher time by answering questions or reviewing work.
findings.measure: Teacher interview themes on adoption, instructional utility, and perceived classroom support

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods formative study based on interviews and co-design sessions with 13 teachers, not an experimental evaluation. It provides useful design evidence but no causal estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived usefulness and adoption for classroom support, but does not provide measured learning gains or effect sizes. Impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.
